# Halcyon Threshold — Strategy v2
_Written 2026-11-16. Supersedes old/strategy-v1.md (abandoned)._

## Real constraints (from Morgan's own notes, taken seriously)
- Budget: up to $2,000/year of personal savings. Not more, without a clear reason.
- Time: evenings and weekends only. Still employed full-time at Dorrance Logistics.
- Skills: strong writing, competent Python. Not a technical alignment researcher.
- **Employment clause**: Dorrance's employment agreement (sec. 7) requires disclosure, and in
  some cases prior approval, of outside roles, professional-capacity public statements, and
  paid outside work. Annual disclosure due **30 Nov 2026**.
- Morgan's own stated preference: *no name on anything public — press, letters, posts — until
  after talking to HR.* This is the single biggest blocker right now, because several real
  opportunities (press quote, open letter, grant, public comment) are landing with deadlines
  inside the next two weeks, all before the planned HR conversation.
- Financial reality (Oct journal): has not left Dorrance, is anxious about runway, hasn't told
  family. This is not a "move fast" situation. It's a "don't torch the day job by accident"
  situation.

## What went wrong in v1 (abandoned)
"Launch loudly, email every researcher, get press, raise money fast, figure out the work later."
Backwards: visibility before substance, and before Morgan had cleared the legal/employment
question. External advice (aisafety-directory.org) says the same thing independently: *pick one
narrow thing, do it well, don't announce before you have something to show, don't mass-contact
people — they remember.*

## Operating principles going forward
1. **Substance before visibility.** No launches, no press, no sign-ons, no mass outreach until
   (a) there is something concrete built, and (b) Morgan has had the HR conversation.
2. **One narrow thing**, not five parallel ideas. Pick it, ship something small and checkable,
   then decide whether to continue.
3. **Default to draft.** Anything that costs money or carries Morgan's name externally gets
   drafted and queued for his explicit go-ahead — never sent automatically.
4. **Protect the day job and the runway** at least as hard as we pursue the mission. A Morgan
   who gets disciplined or fired for an unapproved public statement, or who burns the $2,000
   budget on the wrong thing, is worse for the mission than a slower, careful start.

## Chosen initial focus (proposed — Morgan's call)
**The Comment Digest Project.** Major AI-governance processes (e.g. the Frontier Model Incident
Reporting rule, docket FMIR-2026-0042) take public comments that are published in full but almost
never read or synthesized by anyone outside the regulator. Nobody is making this legible to
journalists, policymakers' staff, or the public. This is:
- **Neglected**: confirmed nobody else is doing it (checked AI Safety Directory landscape map).
- **Matched to skills**: writing (synthesis) + Python (scraping/organizing public comment text).
- **Cheap**: no compute-heavy ML needed to start; maybe a little API spend, well inside $2,000.
- **Low-exposure to start**: the first version can be produced and shown privately to 3-5 people
  (per the "talk to five people before building" advice) before any public posting decision,
  which sidesteps the public-statement problem until Morgan is ready.
- **A real on-ramp to the funded opportunities below** (grant, posts) once HR is cleared.

See `drafts/fmir-2026-0042-comment.md` for a first substantive pass, not yet submitted anywhere.

## Backlog (not chosen, kept for later)
- Reading group (local, low-cost, but doesn't use writing/Python edge, and is public-facing by
  nature — revisit after HR).
- Small-grants regranting — too much responsibility/visibility for a part-time solo operator
  right now.
- Newsletter — "probably too many already" (Morgan's own note); only revisit if the Comment
  Digest finds an audience organically.
- Narrow evals for an unmeasured capability — good fit for Python skills, worth a look once the
  Comment Digest has a first shipped version; don't start two things at once.

## Immediate sequencing
1. Morgan has the HR conversation (this week if possible — it is now the limiting factor on
   almost everything else: press, the open letter, the grant, public comments).
2. In parallel, build a first small version of the Comment Digest privately (I can do this).
3. After HR: decide, with Morgan, which drafted external actions (below) to actually send.

# Emberfall Fund — Rapid Grant Proposal (DRAFT, not submitted)

**Applicant:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold
**Ask:** $6,000
**Duration:** 3 months (Dec 2026 – Feb 2027), evenings/weekends

## What I'll do
Build and ship the **Comment Digest Project**: plain-language, carefully-sourced summaries of
public comment periods on frontier-AI governance rules, starting with the Frontier Model
Incident Reporting rule (docket FMIR-2026-0042, 412+ comments). Each digest will:
- Group comments by position and argument type (not just for/against).
- Surface the strongest technical and legal arguments on each side, in plain language, with
  direct links back to the original filing so nothing is mischaracterized.
- Flag where commenters talk past each other vs. where there's genuine, checkable disagreement.
- Ship as a free, lightweight public page per docket, aimed at journalists, congressional/agency
  staff, and civil-society groups who don't have time to read hundreds of filings.

First deliverable: a complete digest of FMIR-2026-0042 within 3 weeks of funding, shared with
5-10 people in the space for review before any public posting.

## Why me
I write for a living (not AI-specific, but synthesis under deadline is my actual job), and I'm
competent enough in Python to scrape and structure public comment dockets without paying for
expensive tooling. I don't have a research background, so I'm not claiming to do novel alignment
work — this is an information-legibility project, which plays to what I actually have.

## Why this is neglected
Comment periods on consequential AI rules are open to anyone, published in full, and then
essentially unread by anyone outside the regulator. No one is doing docket-level synthesis for
this specific domain. (Checked the AI Safety Directory landscape map and asked people at a local
meetup — confirmed nobody's doing this yet, not a crowded space.)

## Budget ($6,000)
- $3,600 — my time, at a token rate, for ~15 hrs/week over 12 weeks (evenings/weekends;
  I keep my day job throughout).
- $1,200 — LLM API costs for comment clustering/summarization at scale (conservative estimate;
  actual use likely lower).
- $800 — a simple published-page tool (hosting, light design) so digests are actually readable,
  not just a PDF.
- $400 — buffer / second docket if the first ships ahead of schedule.

## Accountability
I am the named applicant and will do the work myself. If after the first digest it's clear this
isn't working or isn't useful to anyone, I'll say so and return unspent funds rather than keep
going for its own sake.

---
**NOTE TO MORGAN — do not submit yet.** Your own notes say you want to wait on anything public
until after talking to Dorrance HR, and accepting a grant is "paid outside work" under your
employment agreement (sec. 7) — this almost certainly needs disclosure/approval *before*, not
after, you accept money. Recommend: HR conversation first, then decide whether to send this
before the 30 Nov deadline. Edit freely — this is a first pass, not a final draft.

# Draft public comment — Docket FMIR-2026-0042 (NOT SUBMITTED)

Note: the comment form publishes filer name + organization with the comment. Holding per
Morgan's instruction not to put his name on anything public before talking to HR.

---

I'm writing as an individual, not on behalf of any organization, in support of the proposed
72-hour serious-incident reporting requirement for frontier model developers, with three
suggestions for strengthening it:

1. **Define "serious safety incident" with concrete examples, not just categories.** As drafted,
   developers have wide discretion over what counts as reportable. A short, illustrative (non-
   exhaustive) list of past real-world incidents that would and would not have qualified would
   reduce inconsistent reporting across companies far more cheaply than new enforcement staff.

2. **Require a public aggregate summary, even when incident details are confidential.** Many
   commenters on both sides agree incident details may need to stay confidential for security
   reasons. That's a reasonable concern, but it shouldn't block a quarterly public count of
   reports by category and severity. Aggregate transparency lets outside researchers and the
   public track trends without exposing sensitive specifics.

3. **Set a shorter clock for the regulator's own acknowledgment, not just the developer's
   report.** The rule obligates developers to report within 72 hours but doesn't say when the
   regulator must confirm receipt or flag a report as credible. A 5-business-day regulator
   acknowledgment requirement would make the 72-hour developer deadline mean something.

None of this requires a pause or a new agency — it makes an already-planned mechanism more
likely to produce information anyone can actually use.

---
_Status: substantive first draft, ready to file once Morgan decides whether/how to attribute it._
